title: Principles of Care for the Hospitalized Child and Integrated Management of Newborn and Childhood Illness (IMNCI / IMCI)
introduction: Hospitalization disrupts a child's routines, sense of safety, and family stability, requiring developmentally tailored preparation, rooming-in, and therapeutic play. At the primary-care and community levels, the WHO/UNICEF Integrated Management of Newborn and Childhood Illness (IMNCI/IMCI) strategy unifies assessment, colour-coded triage, treatment, caregiver counselling, and follow-up to save under-five lives.
learningOutcomes: 8.1 Compare how infants, toddlers, preschoolers, school-age children, and adolescents perceive illness and hospitalization, and identify common reactions (regression, aggression, withdrawal).

8.2 Formulate age-specific preparation plans for hospitalized children and their families, and apply core pediatric hospital nursing principles (preventing separation, minimizing loss of control, rooming-in, and therapeutic play).
8.3 Define IMCI/IMNCI, explain its evolution from single-disease programmes, and detail its three core components and seven principles of integrated care.

8.4 Apply the six-step IMNCI case management process and colour-coded triage system (pink, yellow, green) to assess general danger signs, main symptoms (cough, diarrhoea, fever, ear problems), malnutrition/anaemia, and sick young infants (birth–2 months).
8.5 Explain caregiver counselling, scheduled follow-up reassessment, phased national IMCI implementation, strengths, challenges, and programme evaluation.

content.heading: Hospitalization: Age-Specific Perceptions, Preparation, and Common Reactions
content.body: Whether elective or emergent, hospitalization exposes children to unfamiliar environments, frightening sounds, strange personnel, invasive procedures, and disrupted family coping. Illness and hospitalization carry distinct meanings by developmental stage: (1) Infant—global reaction to disrupted familiar routines/surroundings and separation from the primary love object; (2) Toddler—highest separation anxiety and fear of desertion, relating illness to concrete circumstances; (3) Preschooler—intense fear of bodily harm, mutilation, castration, and intrusive procedures (strong though slightly less separation anxiety than toddlers), often viewing illness as punishment for wrongdoing; (4) School-Age—fears the physical nature of illness and separation from peers/school status, perceiving an external cause located in the body; and (5) Adolescent—anxious about loss of independence, control, identity, and privacy, able to explain illness as organ/process malfunction. Preparation must convey a positive parental attitude and match developmental level: minimal verbal prep for infants (pack favourite toy/blanket, maximize caregiver presence); alleviate toddlers' and preschoolers' three chief fears (unknown, abandonment/separation, mutilation) via favourite toys and doll play; give school-age children and adolescents factual explanations, hospital orientations, and introductions to peers who underwent similar conditions; reassure culturally diverse families of equal care; preserve family/school contact for chronically ill/disabled children via calls, letters, and open visiting; and reduce parental anxiety early by encouraging questions about procedures and length of stay. Three classic behavioural reactions across ages are Regression (reverting to bedwetting, thumb-sucking, clinging, whining), Aggression (crying, yelling, kicking, resisting medicines due to lost control), and Withdrawal (reduced play, speech, appetite, and eye contact).

content.heading: Nursing Care Principles, Coping Strategies, and Therapeutic Play for the Hospitalized Child
content.body: Pediatric hospital nursing centres on three protective principles: (1) Preventing/Minimizing Separation—top priority for children <5 years by welcoming continuous parental presence, supporting anxious children physically, talking frequently about absent parents if detachment occurs, coaching parents on leaving/returning, encouraging frequent visits, and leaving a comforting home item; (2) Minimizing Loss of Control—promoting movement during procedures (on a parent's lap or via wheelchairs/mobile beds), time structuring (co-designing a written daily schedule integrating treatments, schoolwork, and play), encouraging age-appropriate self-care and food/bedtime choices, and anticipatory education on child rights; and (3) Preventing/Minimizing Fear of Bodily Injury—pre-procedure preparation, modified atraumatic techniques, repeated explanations against mutilation fears, and pain reduction. Four structured coping strategies support normal development: Child Life Programs (specialists coordinating age-appropriate medical/playroom sessions), Rooming-In (parents staying in-room on cots/built-in beds to participate in care), Therapeutic Recreation, and Therapeutic Play. Hospital play serves eight functions: diversion/relaxation, security in a strange setting, easing separation/homesickness, releasing tension/emotions, building positive interaction, creative expression, achieving therapeutic goals, and placing the child in an active, choice-making role. Techniques adapt by age: infants enjoy touch/manipulation and pat-a-cake; toddlers need slow parent-present approaches, curtain peek-a-boo (reinforcing object permanence), transitional blankets, repeated stories, dolls, and safe hospital gear (bandages, needleless syringes); preschoolers use body outlines, dolls, puppets, colouring, and play dough to work through aggression/mutilation fears; school-age children use body outlines, accurate anatomical terms, Goodenough draw-a-person assessments (ages 3–13), crafts, games, and collecting disposable care items for mastery; adolescents need peer visits, phone contact, movie/game nights, modified wheelchair basketball, and evening recreational choices. Nurses actively join play through themed storytelling, bath water play, guided TV viewing, needle play, pre/post-op teaching, and art, observing coping without over-policing playroom tidiness.

content.heading: IMNCI / IMCI: Evolution, Philosophy, Three Components, and Principles of Integrated Care
content.body: Preventable neonatal causes (prematurity, birth asphyxia, neonatal sepsis, neonatal tetanus, congenital anomalies, low birth weight) and post-neonatal under-5 killer diseases (pneumonia, diarrhoea, malaria, measles, malnutrition [underlying nearly half of under-5 deaths], anaemia, meningitis, HIV, dengue haemorrhagic fever) account for over 70% of under-5 deaths in low- and middle-income countries. Because sick children typically present with multiple overlapping illnesses that fragmented single-disease programmes missed, WHO and UNICEF launched Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) in 1992/1995 and expanded it to IMNCI to cover the critical neonatal period from birth through 5 years. Treating the whole child holistically across preventive, promotive, curative, and rehabilitative care, IMNCI rests on three pillars: (1) Improving Health Worker Case Management Skills (clinical charts, rational minimum essential medicines, supportive supervision, caretaker counselling); (2) Strengthening Overall Health Systems (essential drug/equipment availability, stock control, supervision, reliable referral transport, follow-up); and (3) Improving Family and Community Health Practices (16 key family practices spanning care-seeking, home care, breastfeeding/nutrition, safe water/sanitation, immunization, and adherence). Its seven integrated care principles mandate: checking every child for general danger signs; routinely assessing major symptoms plus nutrition, immunization, and feeding; using limited evidence-based sensitive/specific signs suited to first-level clinics; assigning severity-based colour-coded classifications rather than isolated diagnoses (Pink = urgent hospital referral/admission after pre-referral treatment; Yellow = specific clinic treatment + home care teaching; Green = home care counselling); recognizing guidelines do not cover acute trauma/injuries; utilizing essential drugs with active caretaker involvement; and prioritizing caretaker counselling.

content.heading: Six-Step IMNCI Case Management Process, Danger Signs, and Main Symptom Classifications
content.body: IMNCI divides children into two age groups—Sick Young Infant (birth/1 week to 2 months) and Sick Child (2 months to 5 years)—following six sequential steps: (1) Assess (ask, look, listen, feel), (2) Classify (colour-coded chart), (3) Identify Treatment, (4) Treat (give first oral dose in clinic while mother watches, teach home care, or give pre-referral treatment + referral note/transport), (5) Counsel the Mother, and (6) Follow Up (usually 2–5 days). For children aged 2 months–5 years, first check the four General Danger Signs: (1) unable to drink or breastfeed, (2) vomits everything, (3) convulsions (now or during this illness), and (4) lethargic or unconscious—ANY one danger sign requires immediate pre-referral treatment (antibiotic, sugar-water, warmth) and urgent hospital referral. Next assess four Main Symptoms: (a) Cough/Difficult Breathing (count breaths for 1 full minute; fast breathing cut-offs: ≥50/min for 2–12 months, ≥40/min for 12 months–5 years; check chest indrawing and calm stridor)—Pink (danger sign or calm stridor -> urgent referral), Yellow (fast breathing or chest indrawing -> Pneumonia: oral amoxicillin + follow-up), Green (no pneumonia signs -> soothe throat, home care); (b) Diarrhoea (ask duration/blood; check lethargy, sunken eyes, drinking eagerly/poorly, skin pinch)—Severe dehydration (Plan C: IV fluids/urgent referral), Some dehydration (Plan B: ORS in clinic over 4 hours), No dehydration (Plan A: extra fluids/feeding at home), ALWAYS adding zinc for 10–14 days and continued feeding; (c) Fever (duration, stiff neck, rash, malaria test)—Very severe febrile disease (danger sign/stiff neck -> urgent referral), Malaria (positive test -> national antimalarial/ACT), Measles (rash + cough/runny nose/red eyes -> Vitamin A), Fever no malaria (home care); and (d) Ear Problem (pain, pus duration, tender mastoid swelling)—Mastoiditis (tender behind-ear swelling -> urgent referral), Acute ear infection (pus <14 days or pain -> antibiotic + dry wick), Chronic ear infection (pus ≥14 days -> dry wick + topical quinolone drops). Always check Malnutrition (MUAC <11.5 cm, severe wasting, or bilateral foot swelling = severe; 11.5 to <12.5 cm = moderate; ≥12.5 cm = normal), Anaemia (severe palmar pallor -> urgent referral), immunization, Vitamin A, and deworming. For Sick Young Infants (birth–2 months), assess Possible Serious Bacterial Infection (PSBI): any ONE of not feeding well, convulsions, fast breathing ≥60/min, severe chest indrawing, fever ≥37.5°C or hypothermia <35.5°C, or moving only when stimulated -> give first antibiotic dose, keep warm, and refer urgently (also assess jaundice, diarrhoea, feeding/weight, and HIV exposure).

content.heading: Counselling, Follow-Up, Implementation, Strengths, Challenges, and Evaluation
content.body: Effective maternal counselling uses active listening, clear demonstration, and teach-back verification covering feeding (exclusive breastfeeding 0–6 months, nutritious complementary foods + continued breastfeeding ≥6 months, extra fluids and continued feeding during illness) and immediate return danger signs (unable to drink/breastfeed, becomes sicker, develops fever, fast/difficult breathing, blood in stool, or drinks poorly). At scheduled follow-up (2–5 days), nurses reassess and act: Improving (complete course, praise mother, reinforce feeding), Not Improving (switch to second-line treatment per chart), or Worse (urgent hospital referral). Introducing IMCI nationally follows six phased steps: adopting integrated child health in national policy, adapting charts to local epidemiology/drugs/language, training first-level clinic staff, securing low-cost essential medicines/equipment, strengthening referral hospitals, and building community support mechanisms (implemented in >75 countries). Strengths include holistic care, rational antibiotic use, simple primary-level charts, and empowered mothers; persistent challenges include training/supervision gaps, drug stock-outs, weak referral transport, and delayed family care-seeking. Multi-country evaluations (Brazil, Bangladesh, Peru, Uganda, Tanzania) assessing impact, cost, and effectiveness show IMCI improves clinician performance and care quality, reduces under-five mortality and improves nutrition when scaled up, and costs up to six times less per correctly managed child than conventional care.

inTextQuestions.question: Which hospitalized age group experiences the highest separation anxiety, and which group commonly interprets illness as punishment for wrongdoing?
inTextQuestions.answer: Toddlers experience the highest separation anxiety and fear of desertion, while preschoolers (and older toddlers) commonly fear bodily mutilation and interpret illness as punishment for wrongdoing.

inTextQuestions.question: What are the IMNCI fast-breathing cut-off rates for young infants (<2 months), infants aged 2–12 months, and children aged 12 months–5 years?
inTextQuestions.answer: Birth to 2 months: 60 or more breaths/min; 2 to 12 months: 50 or more breaths/min; 12 months to 5 years: 40 or more breaths/min.

inTextQuestions.question: What do the three IMNCI colour-coded triage categories (Pink, Yellow, and Green) signify?
inTextQuestions.answer: Pink signifies severe illness requiring pre-referral treatment and urgent hospital referral; Yellow signifies illness needing specific treatment at the facility plus home-care teaching; Green signifies mild illness safely managed with home care and return counselling.

inTextQuestions.question: List the four IMNCI General Danger Signs checked in every sick child aged 2 months to 5 years.
inTextQuestions.answer: Unable to drink or breastfeed, vomits everything, convulsions (currently or during this illness), and lethargic or unconscious.

saqs.question: Explain the meaning of hospitalization to a preschooler and an adolescent, and describe the three common behavioural reactions of children to hospitalization.
saqs.answer: Preschoolers fear bodily harm, mutilation, and intrusive procedures, experience strong separation anxiety, and often view illness as punishment for wrongdoing. Adolescents fear loss of independence, control, identity, and privacy, and understand illness as organ/process malfunction. Common reactions are Regression (reverting to bedwetting, thumb-sucking, clinging), Aggression (crying, kicking, resisting meds over lost control), and Withdrawal (loss of interest, reduced talking/eating, avoiding eye contact).

saqs.question: Outline the core nursing principles for preventing separation and minimizing loss of control in a hospitalized child, and state six functions of hospital play.
saqs.answer: Preventing separation (<5 yrs priority): welcome parents continuously, provide physical presence during anxiety, talk about parents if detached, coach leaving/returning, encourage frequent visits, and leave home comfort articles. Minimizing loss of control: use parent's lap during procedures, wheelchair mobility, written time structuring, self-care/food choices, and child-rights education. Six play functions: diversion/relaxation, security, reducing separation stress, releasing tension/feelings, social interaction, and active choice/mastery (also creative expression and therapeutic goals).

saqs.question: Define IMNCI/IMCI, explain why it was developed to replace single-disease programmes, and state its three core components.
saqs.answer: IMNCI/IMCI is an evidence-based WHO/UNICEF holistic strategy for assessing, classifying, and managing sick newborns and children up to 5 years at first-level facilities and in communities. It replaced fragmented single-disease programmes because sick under-5s frequently suffer multiple overlapping conditions (pneumonia, diarrhoea, malaria, measles, malnutrition, neonatal infections) causing >70% of deaths. Its three components are: (1) improving health worker case management skills, (2) strengthening overall health systems, and (3) improving family and community health practices.

saqs.question: List the six steps of the IMNCI case management process and state the six signs of Possible Serious Bacterial Infection (PSBI) in a sick young infant (birth–2 months) with the required immediate action.
saqs.answer: Six steps: Assess, Classify, Identify treatment, Treat, Counsel the mother, and Follow up. PSBI signs in a young infant (any one suffices): not feeding well, convulsions, fast breathing (≥60/min), severe chest indrawing, fever (≥37.5°C) or low temperature (<35.5°C), and moving only when stimulated. Action: administer the first antibiotic dose, keep the infant warm, and refer urgently to hospital.

saqs.question: Summarize the IMNCI dehydration management plans (A, B, C), maternal counselling points on when to return immediately, and key findings from global IMCI evaluations.
saqs.answer: Diarrhoea plans: Plan A (no dehydration—home extra fluids and continued feeding), Plan B (some dehydration—ORS in clinic over 4 hours), Plan C (severe dehydration—IV fluids or urgent referral), always adding zinc for 10–14 days. Return immediately if unable to drink/breastfeed, becomes sicker, develops fever, fast/difficult breathing, blood in stool, or drinks poorly. Global evaluations (impact, cost, effectiveness) confirm IMCI improves health worker quality, lowers under-5 mortality when scaled up, and costs up to six times less per correctly managed child.
